He says he drove the tram for forty years.

Know that in everyday speech the indicative or Konjunktiv II is used more often.
It's April 2031. A journalist from the Berliner Zeitung, Frau Krüger, has heard about the “singing house” on Kastanienallee. She's interviewing Ludwig in the café “Bei Ingrid”. Mara is listening.
Mr Brandt, thank you very much for taking the time. Our readers want to know why your house is called “the singing house”.
Because almost every evening someone makes music here. There used to be a pianist on the fourth floor. Now there's a teacher with a cello. And me with my guitar, when my fingers let me.
How long have you been the landlord?
Since 1995. I bought the house after the fall of communism, with the money I had saved for forty years. Before that I was a tram driver. Line 46, today the M1.
And is it true that you choose your tenants yourself? People say you even have a special paragraph in the tenancy agreement.
It's true. Anyone who moves in here has to promise to make music at the courtyard party. I'm an old man. I don't have time any more for neighbours who don't know each other.
What's the most important thing for you in this house?
That nobody is alone. When my wife died, I was alone. Then a young nurse from Romania came along. She showed me that you're never too old to let new people into your life.
Is that the woman sitting over there by the window?
Yes. But don't write that. Otherwise she'll blush.
“zye” (Konj. I of sein), “HAH-buh” (Konj. I of haben).
A French word: “zhoor-nah-LIS-tin”, with the “j” as in “measure”.
When you report what someone else said without saying whether it's true, the press and official texts use Konjunktiv I. That way the journalist shows: “HE said this, not me”.
In everyday speech you simply say: “Ludwig sagt, dass er glücklich ist.” Konjunktiv I is something you mainly need to RECOGNISE in newspapers and on the news.
It's formed from the infinitive stem + -e. It's used most often in the third person singular:
“sein” is irregular in all persons: ich sei, du sei(e)st, er sei, wir seien, ihr seiet, sie seien.
He says he has no time.
She declares that she's coming tomorrow.
He claims he drove the tram for forty years. (past: sei + participle)
When Konjunktiv I looks the same as the indicative (especially in the plural and with “ich”), Konjunktiv II is used, so that it's clear it's indirect speech:
People say you have a special paragraph.
Sie fragt, ob er Zeit habe.
Er sagt, sie solle das nicht schreiben.
Commands (the imperative) are reported with “sollen”: “Komm!” → Er sagt, ich solle kommen. Polite requests with “mögen”: Er bittet, man möge leise sein.
Typical press expressions: laut + dative (laut Ludwig = according to Ludwig), angeblich (allegedly), wie er betont (as he stresses).

The singing house. How an old block of flats in Prenzlauer Berg became a family. By Katrin Krüger. At Kastanienallee 31 there is no sign to show it. But anyone who stands in the courtyard at nine in the evening, under the big chestnut tree, hears music. Sometimes a cello, sometimes a guitar, sometimes children singing from a window on the second floor. The neighbours call it “the singing house”.

The landlord, Ludwig Brandt, is eighty-two. He says he was a tram driver for forty years, on line 46, which today is called the M1. After the fall of communism, he says, he bought the house with his savings. Back then it was apparently in a bad state, with broken windows and a roof that let the rain in. “I repaired it, flat by flat,” he recounts. His wife, Ingrid, apparently chose the tenants. She died, he says, in 2021.

According to Brandt, after her death everything changed. He was alone, he says, hardly spoke to the neighbours any more and even stopped playing the guitar. “Every evening I sat in front of the television and waited for the day to pass,” he says. Then, in the autumn of 2026, a young woman apparently rang his doorbell. She only wanted to collect her keys.

This young woman is Mara Ionescu, now thirty-one, a nurse from Sibiu, Romania. She works on a ward of a Berlin hospital and is now training to become a ward manager. Speaking to our newspaper, she stresses that she didn't do anything special. “I just asked people how they were. And then I listened.” Her neighbours see things differently.

Lena Brandt, the landlord's granddaughter, who runs a bakery on the ground floor and, since November, the café “Bei Ingrid”, says that Mara “brought her grandfather back to life”. She apparently taught him to use a smartphone and took him to concerts. She even arranged for him to drive a historic tram one more time on his eightieth birthday, Lena says. “Without Mara, Grandpa would still be sitting in front of the television today,” says Lena. “And I would never have met my boyfriend. He's her brother.”

Until two months ago, the best-known resident of the house was Margarete Hoffmann, ninety-four, once one of the most important pianists in the GDR. She lived on the fourth floor for sixty years. Every evening at nine, the neighbours say, she played with the window open. The children from the second floor, Kuba and Ola Nowak, now twelve, say that for years they fell asleep to this music. “I thought it was normal,” says Ola. “That all houses have music.”

Mrs Hoffmann's story is one of the most moving this newspaper has heard in recent years. In 1961, it is said, she was separated by the building of the Wall from the great love of her life, the violinist Friedrich Mertens. She apparently never sent a letter she wrote to him. Sixty-five years later, Mara Ionescu is said to have read this letter, and her brother Andrei, a computer science student at the TU Berlin, is said to have found Mertens in Lübeck. Today the two of them live together in a care home two streets from here. Mr Mertens says he is ninety-six and happier than ever.

Mrs Hoffmann's grand piano now stands in the primary school on Kastanienallee. The music teacher Jakob Lorenz, who since March has been living with Mara Ionescu on the fourth floor, declares that since then the children have been twice as interested in music. Once a month, he says, Mrs Hoffmann comes to the school in person and gives an hour's lesson. “She's strict,” says a boy from Year 4. “But she says mistakes are allowed. The important thing is to keep playing.”

At the end of the conversation, we ask Ludwig Brandt what he would advise other landlords in Berlin. He thinks for a long time. Then he says that you shouldn't only look at the rent, but at the people. A house, he says, is not a building but a community. “Ask your tenants how they are,” he says. “And then listen. It costs nothing. And it's the best thing I've learnt in eighty-two years.” We ask who he learnt it from. Ludwig Brandt smiles and looks towards the window, where a young woman is sitting with a coffee, pretending not to listen. “That,” he says, “please don't write.” We wrote it anyway.

The article appeared on a Saturday in May, over a whole page, with a large photograph of Ludwig under the chestnut tree, with Fritz at his feet. Lena bought twenty copies of the newspaper and hung one, framed, next to the till, beside Grandma Ingrid's quotation. Ludwig pretended to be embarrassed. But Mara saw him reading the article again every morning over his coffee, slowly, with his finger under the lines. On Monday the first visitors came who had read the article. They stood in the courtyard, looked up at the windows and asked Lena whether there would be music that evening. Lena told them it depended on whether Jakob felt like it. Jakob felt like it.

Two weeks later a letter arrived, addressed to “Mr Ludwig Brandt, Kastanienallee 31, the singing house”. The sender was a woman from Hamburg, Gisela Weber, aged eighty-five. She wrote that she had read the article and absolutely had to tell him something. In August 1961, she wrote, she had been visiting relatives in the West when the Wall was built. Her parents had stayed in the East, on Kastanienallee. She hadn't seen her mother for twenty-eight years. Her mother had later told her that she took the tram on line 46 every day and that a young tram driver with long hair always kept her a window seat, on the side from which you could see towards the West. He never asked why, she wrote. He simply smiled every morning. “I believe,” Mrs Weber wrote, “that you were that tram driver. My mother died in 1995. But she talked about you until the end. Thank you for the window seat.” Ludwig read the letter at the kitchen table, under the yellow lamp. Then he handed it to Mara and went out with Fritz without a word. He was gone for two hours. When he came back, all he said was: “I remember her. She always wore a red scarf. I knew why she looked out of the window. Everyone knew. But you weren't allowed to say it.”

The next day, Ludwig replied to her. By hand, in ink, in his large, shaky handwriting, three pages long. It took him the whole afternoon. Mara didn't ask what he wrote. But when she took the letter to the post office, she saw that he had put something small in the envelope: an old, yellowed tram ticket for line 46, from 1975, which he had kept in a drawer for fifty years. On the back he had written: “For your mother. Window seat. Always free.”
Wann hat Ludwig das Haus gekauft?
Sie habe ihren Großvater zurück ins Leben geholt.
Was dachten Kuba und Ola als Kinder?
